doc.title: Pete Candoli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Trying Les Brown, then Miller band; why musicians left bands
summary: Pete quickly leaves Les Brown for musical reasons, joins Tex Beneke's Miller band, and discusses why players changed bands often.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: I remember like in ’48 I remember joining Tex Benecke in the Miller band, because Goz says, “Come on the band,” you know, “you’ve got to come on the band.” So I did that. Well before that I was back on the west coast and I joined Les Brown and went the Rich’s Garden was the first gig and we were there and after about a week — and he was such a wonderful guy — I said, “Look, Les, I don’t think I’m going to be traveling.” He said, “Well we’re giving you billing as the feature, you’re taking Jimmy Zito’s book with the solos.” I said, this was after the first Herd, I said, “I don’t think I’m going to be happy, maybe you ought to get somebody else, Les, because I know what kind of music I like to play.” He says, “Pete, whatever you want, but we’d sure love to have you stay.”
I see. Musically it wasn’t something you thought you could—

You know I’ve got to be very honest, I mean it felt like an overblown hotel band, you understand. There were five brass or three trumpets and a trombone and four sax, they had eight brass you know. But it didn’t go too far above, as far as I was concerned. I was too interested in playing, and getting into things.

You know when you look at the bios of the different guys in the big bands, it seems that there’s about a two year period where — let me rephrase this — it seems that not often does a guy stick with a band for more than two or three years. I mean is it partly economic? Is it partly the music?

Well maybe both. I would think, if they felt like me, it was principally music. Because I’d rather play for less and know that like something was happening you see. But different bands afforded a good livelihood to musicians, especially the hotel bands that stayed in one spot for six weeks. That was a long time. It seems like a lifetime, the way bands were going back and forth in those days. And I think some had kids you know, being away from kids and others wanted to continue their academic ways, and maybe wind up teaching.
Sure. Because you were really young men at that time.
You were 16 when you were playing—
Oh yeah, let’s say when I first, well right at Purdue when I did the things with Will Bradley at the campus there, in the second year.
